story917:
Iktomi the spider trickster wrapped himself in a fine robe and went walking. He was feeling generous — a rare and dangerous state for Iktomi, for his generosity usually came with strings attached.

He came upon a large boulder sitting in the middle of the trail. "You must be cold," Iktomi said to the boulder. "Here — take my robe."

The boulder did not respond. It was a boulder.

"I insist," Iktomi said, draping the robe across the boulder's surface. "A fine robe like this deserves a fine recipient."

Iktomi walked away, feeling virtuous. But when the wind picked up and the air grew cold, he wanted his robe back. He returned to the boulder.

"I have come for my robe," he said.

The boulder did not respond.

"My robe," Iktomi repeated, tugging at the fabric. It did not move. The boulder had absorbed the robe into itself, as boulders do.

Iktomi grew angry. "You ungrateful stone! I gave you my finest robe and you refuse to return it!"

He insulted the boulder. He kicked it. He scratched at it with his spider claws.

The boulder, who had patience but not infinite patience, began to move. It rolled toward Iktomi, slowly at first, then faster. Iktomi ran, but the boulder was relentless. It caught him and crushed him flat.

Iktomi lay in the dust, flattened like a pressed leaf. He could not move. He could not speak. He could only watch as the sky wheeled overhead.

Bats came to help. They flew down from the rocks and pecked at the boulder with their tiny teeth. They pecked and pecked until the boulder cracked open, and Iktomi slid free.

But the bats' faces were smashed flat in the effort. To this day, bats have flattened faces — a reminder of the time they saved the trickster who could not save himself.

Iktomi, ever ungrateful, scattered pebbles across the plains as he walked away. The pebbles became the stones that cover the land, and Iktomi never wore a robe again.
story918:
White Buffalo Calf Woman gave the Lakota people not just the sacred pipe but seven rites — seven ceremonies that would guide their spiritual life from birth to death and beyond.

The first rite is the Keeping of the Soul. When a loved one dies, a lock of their hair is kept in a sacred bundle for a year. During that year, the soul is preserved — held in the safety of the bundle while it adjusts to the spirit world. After a year of mourning and ceremony, the soul is released to travel the Sky-Road to the happy hunting ground.

The second rite is the Purification Rite — the sweat lodge ceremony. A dome of willow branches is covered with hides, and heated stones are placed in a pit at the center. Water is thrown on the stones, filling the lodge with steam. Participants sit in the darkness, sweating, praying, cleansing their bodies and spirits of impurities.

The third rite is Crying for a Vision — the vision quest. A young person goes alone to a hilltop or remote place and fasts for four days, praying for guidance. The spirits may come in the form of animals, clouds, or visions, each one carrying a message for the seeker.

The fourth rite is the Sun Dance — the annual renewal ceremony. A sacred pole is erected, and dancers attach themselves to it with skewers, offering their blood and their prayers. They dance for four days, looking only at the sun, their sacrifice renewing the covenant between the people and the Creator.

The fifth rite is the Making of Relatives — an adoption ceremony that binds two families together. The sixth is the Girls' Coming of Age — a ceremony that honors a young woman's transition to womanhood. The seventh is the Throwing of the Ball — a game that symbolizes the Creator's love, the ball thrown upward representing the soul's ascent.

Each rite uses the sacred pipe given by the White Buffalo Calf Woman. Each rite connects the Lakota people to the spiritual forces that govern their world. Together, the seven rites form a complete spiritual framework — a guide for living well, dying well, and existing well in the spirit world beyond.
story919:
Two Lakota girls lay outside their tipi one summer night, gazing at the sky. The stars were brilliant — thousands of them scattered across the darkness like seeds thrown by a generous hand.

One girl pointed at the brightest star. "I wish I could marry that one," she said, laughing.

The other girl pointed at the Morning Star. "And I wish I could marry that one."

They fell asleep with their wishes on their lips. But the stars heard. The brightest star and the Morning Star descended from the sky while the girls slept, and when the girls awoke, they found themselves in the sky world.

The first girl was the wife of the brightest star. His home was beautiful — walls of light, floors of silver, a roof made of the deepest night sky. But everything was strange. The food tasted of starlight, not of earth. The water tasted of distance, not of rivers.

The star husband warned her: "There is one rule. You must never dig around a certain root — a turnip-like root that grows in the garden."

The girl agreed. But curiosity — that oldest and most dangerous of human qualities — overcame her. She dug around the root. When she pulled it up, she saw a hole through the floor of the sky world. Far below, she could see the earth — the plains, the rivers, the smoke rising from the tipis.

She was homesick. She wept, and her tears fell through the hole like rain.

Her star husband found her weeping and understood. He could not keep her against her will — the stars do not hold prisoners. Together they wove a rope of basswood bark, long enough to reach the earth.

The girl began to descend. But the rope was too short. It ended thirty feet above the ground, and the girl fell. She survived — the earth caught her gently — but she was changed. She was no longer entirely of the sky world, and no longer entirely of the earth. She walked among her people, but her eyes were always turned upward, always searching.

Her star husband remained in the sky, visible as the evening star, shining brightest in the west just after sunset — watching, waiting, remembering the wife who chose the earth over the stars.
